articles.title: Connective Resource Mobilization: A Relational Approach to Movement Continuity in Transnational Activism
articles.abstract: Social movement studies have long centered social movement organizations (SMOs) as the primary vehicles of mobilization. Yet contemporary movements are increasingly decentralized and digitally mediated, challenging SMO-centric frameworks such as resource mobilization theory (RMT). As contention becomes more individualized and non-conventional, organization- and event-centered approaches struggle to explain how movements persist, evolve, or dissolve under shifting conditions. Drawing on RMT and economic sociology, this article advances a relational resource mobilization framework through four propositions: resource mobilization (1) is historically contingent; (2) translates into tactics differently across organizational configurations; (3) is relational; and (4) provides an analytic for examining movement continuity across time and space. Within this framework, I introduce the model of connective resource mobilization to theorize how digitally mediated movements generate strategic capacity through personalized earmarking practices across borders and phases of contention. Based on 179 interviews and observation at 187 events in Hong Kong and Canada, I trace how the Hong Kong Pro-Democracy Movement evolved from its 2019 protest peak through its subsequent downturn across domestic and diasporic contexts. The analysis demonstrates how a relational approach to resource mobilization can illuminate divergent trajectories of movement continuity across historical, geographic, political, and socio-technological contexts.

articles.title: Enduring links: mental health effects of ex-partner’s life events among separated parents
articles.authors: Philipp Dierker, Mine Kühn, Sanna Kailaheimo-Björkqvist, Mikko Myrskylä
articles.abstract: Union dissolutions between parents do not necessarily end interdependencies between them. This study examines whether life events of ex-partners with a shared child affect each other’s mental health, extending life course theory on linked lives beyond intact families. Using Finnish population register data from 1987 to 2020 and panel data methods, including two-way fixed effects and dynamic difference-in-differences models, the analysis follows separated parents of minor children and tracks psychotropic medication purchases as an indicator of mental health. The findings reveal that ex-partners’ stepfamily formation events, like re-partnering and childbirth, are followed by modest improvements in mental health, whereas adverse health events experienced by the ex-partner, including cancer diagnosis and death, lead to declines in mental health, particularly among mothers. More distant life events, like the ex-partner’s parent’s death, show no consistent associations. The results demonstrate that parents’ lives remain interdependent after union dissolution, thereby extending the linked lives concept within the life course framework to encompass post-separation family ties.

Insufficient Effort Responding and Adolescent Respondents: Measurement, Extent, and Prediction
articles.authors: Thomas Krause, Susanne Vogl, Christine Sälzer
articles.abstract: This article addresses insufficient effort responding (IER), an issue in survey research affecting data quality. We focus on predicting reactive-check-based IER classifications through nonreactive measures and estimating the proportion of respondents classified as IER in a pupil population, using a sizeable adolescent survey. The analysis highlights IER as a nonmarginal issue that varies considerably by gender, migration status, and school type. Utilizing Random Forest models, we evaluate nonreactive measures’ predictive power for reactive-check-based IER classifications, notably response time, intraindividual response variability, and Mahalanobis Distance. The findings show these measures’ future research value, emphasizing the strong influence of response time. We also explore the relationship between predictors and our target variable and find that shorter response times and less response variability correspond to a greater likelihood of IER. This study illustrates the potential of nonreactive measures and advanced machine learning techniques for identifying IER and highlights the necessity for further research.

articles.title: Do Respondents’ Commitments Improve Data Quality in Opt-in Online Surveys? An International Experiment on Participants’ Attentiveness, Cheating, Satisficing, and Skipping
articles.abstract: Online surveys are increasingly the norm in public opinion research. Self-administered internet surveys present opportunities, but also specific risks for data quality. In search of solutions, scholars are returning to commitment as one way of encouraging participants to provide accurate responses. This article provides an extensive study of commitment as a potential method for improving data quality in the context of opt-in online surveys. Theoretically, I argue that the effectiveness of commitment in motivating good conduct depends on respondents’ material and immaterial cost-benefit calculations. In an experimental survey in 2021 including more than 32,000 respondents from the general populations of 10 countries worldwide, I find that commitments make participants less likely to cheat on knowledge questions, but are ineffective or even counterproductive with respect to respondents’ attentiveness, satisficing, and skipping. Researchers should thus use commitments carefully and selectively, particularly in the context of opt-in online surveys.
